title: Risk Outlook Report: The Use of Artificial Intelligence in the Legal Market
author: Solicitors Regulation Authority

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Legal copilot: Verification costs define practical value
st.an: The source supports legal AI’s drafting, summarisation and potential efficiency or affordability benefits, but presents these largely as examples and predictions. It does not assess output quality, hallucination, grounding or human verification costs, so it does not establish a position on the cluster’s principal claim that verification determines practical value.
qs: Generative systems such as ChatGPT can also automatically summarise online information and draft basic documents on request.
Its increasing availability makes it easier for firms to use it to provide services more affordably, effectively and efficiently than before.

st.t: Firm adoption: Access outruns dependable integration
st.an: The report accepts the cluster’s core distinction between AI availability and dependable operational integration, and materially develops it by identifying skills, support and maintenance costs beyond purchase price and recommending needs-led technology selection. It also adds nuance that small firms may adopt generic or off-the-shelf tools despite resource constraints.
qs: Acquiring the skills and expertise needed to fully understand and use any products can also carry costs, as can the ongoing support and maintenance of the system.
Firms can help to control their own costs in adopting AI by understanding their own business needs first, and then considering if AI may play a role in addressing these.

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s implementation-focused proposition and materially extends it with concrete operational safeguards: staff understanding and training, client transparency, documented explainability, responsible data practices, and ongoing monitoring for bias and inaccuracy. It provides guidance rather than empirical evidence that these measures improve outcomes.
qs: ### Transparency and explainability  - Make sure that you, and staff who can access the system, can understand how it operates and makes decisions, and that you can explain this to clients.

- Monitor the outputs of an AI carefully to make sure it is [not producing biased or inaccurate outcomes.](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/artificial-intelligence/guidance-on-ai-and-data-protection/how-do-we-ensure-fairness-in-ai/)

st.t: AI insurance: Coverage cannot replace professional governance
st.an: The report supports the cluster’s position that insurance coverage is evolving and requires insurer coordination, while effective risk management still depends on professional governance through careful system selection, testing, training and supervision. It offers practical recommendations rather than evidence about claims prevalence, pricing or insurance outcomes.
qs: As a relatively new and rapidly developing tool, the insurance market’s approach to covering the use of legal AI is still emerging.
- Train and supervise your staff in what is and is not a safe and acceptable use of your systems and other uses of AI.

st.t: EU governance: Simplification tests enforceable safeguards
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s view that standards and guidance can provide practical AI risk-management infrastructure, while offering no evidence that these resources are effective or sufficient to establish acceptable risk or enforceable safeguards.
qs: The International Standards Organisation (ISO) has released a [regulatory standard for managing risks from AI](https://www.dataguidance.com/news/international-iso-publishes-guidance-ai-risk-management).
This aims to help users of AI to identify risks, and to integrate risk management into their AI implementation.

st.t: Generative automation: Fluent work product still needs authority
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account that generative AI produces substantive legal work and may improve service delivery or enable new business models. It presents the broader benefits as prospective and firm-dependent rather than established outcomes. It does not, however, directly address the cluster’s central requirements of authoritative grounding, human verification, supervision, and professional responsibility.
qs: This involves directly producing content, such as contract drafting, client letters or any other form of written communication or document.
Used creatively in ways that suit individual firms’ needs, it might also help them to develop new business models that could not exist without it, and even contribute to career satisfaction.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The report supports the cluster’s access-oriented core: AI can automate bounded tasks, increase provider capacity, lower costs and potentially improve accessibility, while solicitors retain oversight and apply expertise where needed. Its evidence is mainly examples, reported benefits and conditional predictions, however, and it does not substantively examine the cluster’s central concern that direct-to-consumer use shifts reliability and verification risks onto unrepresented users.
qs: By automating time consuming routine tasks and basic document drafting, solicitors should be able to apply their experience and knowledge where it is really needed.
It could also make legal services more accessible for those with lower incomes and small businesses.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The SRA aligns closely with the cluster’s core proposition: current legal AI primarily augments human work on bounded tasks, while effective adoption depends on skills, supervision, data controls and verification. Its more optimistic predictions about productivity, cost and access are qualified rather than contrary, though it gives little attention to apprenticeship and deskilling risks.
qs: The government expects its proposals on AI regulation will [encourage investment into the UK, supporting growth.](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/prime-minister-calls-for-global-responsibility-to-take-ai-risks-seriously-and-seize-its-opportunities)  In most systems already in use which employ AI, the technology acts to support and improve the work of humans.
However well controlled and understood a system is, firms will still need to check its outputs for accuracy.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The report supports the cluster’s core view that AI can drive operating-model change rather than merely improve individual productivity. It anticipates new service structures, multidisciplinary skills and client-focused reorganisation under firm oversight, while treating benefits as prospective and offering little evidence on provider bargaining shifts, pricing or quantified returns.
qs: However, it can also help them structure their business in new ways.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The SRA aligns with the cluster’s supervised-aid framing: firms remain accountable for AI outputs, must understand system limitations, verify generated content, protect confidentiality and privilege, and maintain consumer safeguards. It supports innovation and affordability, but treats these benefits as conditional on effective oversight rather than autonomous reliance.
qs: ### Accountability  As with any other technology or system in your firm, you will remain responsible and accountable for the outputs from AI you are using.
- You should also consider what processes you need to put in place to check and verify any information or content being produced through the AI.

st.t: Supervisory accountability: Verification must test substantive support
st.an: The report supports the cluster’s core supervisory-accountability proposition by warning that high-volume AI output can impede effective supervision and requiring firms to maintain processes to manage that risk. It also aligns on fabricated authorities and confidentiality, though it does not develop the cluster’s more specific requirement that verification test the substantive support for legal propositions.
qs: Firms will need to maintain processes that let them manage this issue.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The report strongly aligns with the cluster’s core proposition: legal AI should selectively automate suitable routine tasks while lawyers retain judgment and accountability. It also emphasizes verification, supervision, training, data controls and governance as prerequisites for safe, effective deployment, while treating productivity and access gains as conditional or prospective rather than evidence of general competence or wholesale lawyer replacement.
qs: - Use systems to speed up and automate routine tasks, supporting rather than replacing human judgment.
However well controlled and understood a system is, firms will still need to check its outputs for accuracy.

kp.k: Adoption is spreading beyond the largest law firms
kp.d: The report presents AI as increasingly affordable and commercially available to smaller firms, including through informal staff use. Under its 'end of last year' framing, it reports that three quarters of the largest solicitors’ firms used AI, nearly twice the number three years earlier; over 60% of large firms and a third of small firms were exploring generative systems. Evidence of rising use in small and medium firms is expressly anecdotal.
qs: Dedicated AI for legal work was once only accessible by the largest firms. This is no longer the case.
three quarters of the largest solicitors’ firms were using AI, nearly twice the number from just three years ago
Anecdotal evidence suggests that the use of AI in small and medium firms is also rising.

kp.k: AI spans compliance, administration, search, profiling and drafting
kp.d: Using LawtechUK’s categories, the report describes applications ranging from AML checks and outcome prediction to client intake, document classification, discovery, contract review and written content generation. These categories overlap within products. Chatbots can extend availability and triage cases, while search tools provide an initial step in case preparation rather than a complete replacement for legal work.
qs: It is worth remembering that individual systems can include aspects of several, or all of these at the same time.

They can respond quickly to enquiries from potential clients and potentially offer a 24/7 service for answering common legal questions, gathering and sorting information and triaging cases for seriousness and urgency.
This involves directly producing content, such as contract drafting, client letters or any other form of written communication or document.

kp.k: Reported efficiencies include vendor claims and cross-sector examples
kp.d: The report carries a provider’s claimed 90% case-outcome prediction accuracy, an insurance decision system reportedly taking a third less time than a human and reducing processing costs by 77%, and a global bank example in which AI expanded review from at most 15% of transactions by 120 staff to all files in real time. Contract-tool designers claim savings of three or more hours per signing or renewal. These are attributed examples, not a uniform evaluation of legal AI.
qs: Built so users can understand its reasoning, it takes a third less time than a human to reach decisions. It is said to have reduced the cost of processing claims by 77%.
Before introducing the system, their team of 120 staff could sample at most 15% of their transactions. With the system, they could review all files in real time.
Its designers claim that it can save three or more hours per contract signing/renewal for the client.

kp.k: Automation should redirect lawyers toward judgment-intensive work
kp.d: The report’s recommended model is augmentation: automate routine administration and basic drafting so solicitors can apply expertise to more demanding tasks. It identifies particular potential benefits for small firms whose senior practitioners lack administrative support. It also reports broader worker-survey findings of improved performance and working conditions, without presenting these as a legal-sector-specific finding.
qs: By automating time consuming routine tasks and basic document drafting, solicitors should be able to apply their experience and knowledge where it is really needed.
This could be particularly beneficial for small firms where senior practitioners do not have support from an administrative team.
Use systems to speed up and automate routine tasks, supporting rather than replacing human judgment.

kp.k: Lower delivery costs could improve access to justice
kp.d: The report predicts that reducing time spent per case could lower costs for firms and consumers and make services more accessible to lower-income people and small businesses. It also suggests that explainable outcome prediction could improve prioritisation and encourage earlier settlement. These are conditional opportunities, not demonstrated access-to-justice outcomes.
qs: Automating administrative tasks or certain aspects of cases can lower the time spent, and therefore lower the cost of the work, on each case.
It could also make legal services more accessible for those with lower incomes and small businesses.
the speed, cost and productivity benefits that they can provide could help to improve access to justice.

kp.k: AI may enable new business models and competitive pressure
kp.d: The report suggests firms could offer out-of-hours chatbot services, commercialise internally developed systems under their oversight and reorganise operations using cost savings. It predicts increasingly technology-savvy consumers will expect AI-enabled service improvements and argues that non-adoption may itself become a risk. It does not specify a resulting pricing model or staffing structure.
qs: An AI system developed internally for a firm’s own use could prove to have additional value as a service provided to others under the firm’s oversight.
The risk to firms might not come from adopting AI, but from failing to do so.
Ever more technologically savvy consumers will also increasingly expect firms to use technological tools that improve services.

kp.k: Technology competence and multidisciplinary working become more important
kp.d: Solicitors need not become programmers, but the report says they must understand their systems sufficiently to use and supervise them. It cites research associating AI use with multidisciplinary teams, including IT specialists, and identifies potential professional-development benefits. Commercial products may reduce specialist data-skill requirements, but do not remove supervision needs; prompt engineering is presented as learnable.
qs: Solicitors do not have to be programmers to work with AI. However, they do need to have some understanding of how their systems work.
Firms will still need to be able to understand how data is being used and to be able to supervise the operation of systems.
This will help to increase individuals’ confidence in using advanced technologies, and might help with career satisfaction and professional development.

kp.k: Bias can reproduce discrimination and threaten legal outcomes
kp.d: The report warns of miscarriages of justice and damage to recruitment diversity. Its hypothetical AML example explains how demographic proxies may be mistaken for business-risk factors; historical bias in precedents and legislation is identified as harder to control. As cross-sector evidence, it reports that US mortgage algorithms were 40 per cent more likely to deny minority ethnic borrowers because of historically biased training decisions. It recommends ongoing monitoring because bias can emerge as models evolve.
qs: This could lead to inadvertent discrimination.
Another cause is social biases in the reasoning behind precedents and legislation. This could be harder to control.
Be aware that AI bias can be subtle, and that bias that did not exist when the system was first introduced might develop as the system’s models evolve.

kp.d: The report explains generative errors through text prediction without a concept of reality and cites incidents involving nonexistent cases in AI-drafted arguments. It warns that inaccurate products can harm consumers and inadvertently mislead courts. Controlling data access may reduce problems, but cannot eliminate output checking; firms should not rely on a model to certify its own accuracy.
qs: That is because they work by anticipating the text that should follow the input they are given, but do not have a concept of ‘reality’.
However well controlled and understood a system is, firms will still need to check its outputs for accuracy.
You should also consider what processes you need to put in place to check and verify any information or content being produced through the AI.

kp.k: High output magnifies harm and burdens supervision
kp.d: AI’s speed is both a productivity benefit and a risk multiplier: a system’s errors can affect more people than an individual’s errors, while its volume makes effective supervision harder. The report therefore recommends supervision processes capable of keeping pace with automated production.
qs: Errors by an AI system could affect many more people than errors by a single person could.
Have supervision systems that can cope with the increased speed of AI.

kp.k: Confidentiality and data protection constrain AI deployment
kp.d: The report identifies risks from casual online use on client matters, transferring confidential material to providers for training and outputs exposing details from other cases. It says confidentiality, privilege and data protection remain applicable. Recommendations include controlling transfers, considering synthetic training data, observing individual data rights and checking cloud-storage jurisdictions.
qs: Firms adopting AI will need to make sure that their use of it protects confidentiality and legal privilege.
The ICO is clear that consumers’ data protection rights remain when their information is used for training or operating an AI.
Be careful when transferring data to a cloud based system if you are not certain in which jurisdiction the data will be held.

kp.k: Firms retain accountability for outsourced AI advice
kp.d: The SRA states that firms remain responsible for AI outputs, including errors in initial advice delivered by third-party chatbots. Accountability cannot be shifted to providers or IT teams. Firms must establish supervision and inform clients appropriately about AI involvement; the report leaves the method of communication to each firm’s circumstances.
qs: As with any other technology or system in your firm, you will remain responsible and accountable for the outputs from AI you are using.
For example, if you use a third party chatbot to provide initial legal advice, you remain responsible for any errors in that advice.
Tell clients when you will be using AI with their case, and how it will operate.

kp.k: Transparency and contestability should accompany automated decisions
kp.d: The report argues that explainable, audited AI could clarify legal reasoning and that translation tools could improve communication with non-English-speaking clients. Its recommendations require staff understanding, documented system operation, records identifying AI inferences, routes to contest decisions and complaints procedures able to address AI use. These transparency benefits are conditional, not properties attributed to every system.
qs: Although it is not always easy, it can be possible to show how an AI algorithm is reaching its decisions.
Provide routes for people to contest AI decisions they disagree with.
Make sure that your complaints procedures can handle questions about AI use.

kp.k: Adoption barriers extend beyond software purchase costs
kp.d: The report identifies uncertainty about benefits, regulatory compliance and client acceptance; costs of skills, support and maintenance; limited digitised legal information; and emerging insurance arrangements. It says only the largest firms hold enough data to train their own systems. Suggested responses include starting from business needs, considering commercial or generic tools, collaborating with partners and engaging insurers.
qs: Acquiring the skills and expertise needed to fully understand and use any products can also carry costs, as can the ongoing support and maintenance of the system.
Only the largest firms will hold enough data to train their own systems.
Firms will need to engage closely with their insurers to make sure that misunderstandings do not cause unnecessary costs.

kp.k: Safe adoption requires testing and rules for informal use
kp.d: Organised around the proposed national AI strategy’s five principles, the report recommends careful procurement, clear allocation of technical-error responsibility, predeployment testing, staff training and supervision. Even firms that have not adopted AI need policies addressing staff use of public tools, distinguishing casual online use from approved systems.
qs: Test all systems thoroughly before bringing them into use.
Even if you have not adopted AI as part of your business, staff might still want to use ChatGPT or similar systems. You will need clear rules covering this.
Make sure your supervision and guidance cover the difference between casual use of online AI such as ChatGPT and using systems you have formally adopted.

kp.k: SRA favours outcome-based regulation with innovation support
kp.d: The SRA describes a technology-neutral approach that balances consumer protection with innovation rather than endorsing products. It identifies authorisation of new business models, rule waivers and innovation support as available mechanisms, and reports a 2023–2024 business-plan commitment to develop a sandbox for testing technologies including AI. The sandbox is a plan at the report’s publication date.
qs: Our regulation focuses on the outcomes firms’ actions produce, not necessarily the tools they use to reach them.
waivers for some rules to test new technologies
We intend to retain an open mind on the systems used, balancing protections for consumers with support for innovation.

kp.k: International regulatory divergence creates compliance and advisory demands
kp.d: As of November 2023, the report contrasts the UK’s proposed relatively light-touch approach with the EU AI Act’s anticipated differentiated restrictions and describes the US as just beginning to consider its approach. It recommends that internationally operating firms manage these differences and advise clients while recognising that rules may change quickly.
qs: At the time of writing, the US has just begun considering its own regulatory approach.
Firms that operate internationally will need to manage these regulatory differences and advise their clients appropriately, noting that regulations might develop quickly.

kp.k: Deepfakes threaten fraud detection and evidential confidence
kp.d: The report predicts that realistic generated images, videos and voice imitation will make phishing harder to recognise. It also warns of fabricated evidence and reports at least one instance of a respondent suggesting opposing evidence was AI-falsified. That example concerns an allegation challenging evidence, not an established finding of fabrication.
qs: this is likely to make phishing scams harder to recognise.
In the same way, AI might be used to create false evidence.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The SRA claims that AI adoption is widening beyond large firms and predicts continued growth, efficiency gains, new service models and potentially improved access to justice, alongside material risks requiring human supervision.
pts.d: The SRA reports that commercial and inexpensive online products are making AI accessible to smaller firms, including through informal staff use. It describes existing applications in compliance, case prediction, client intake and triage, document classification, discovery, contract review and drafting. It argues that automation can increase capacity, reduce time and costs, and free solicitors for work requiring their expertise. Lower costs could make services more accessible to lower-income individuals and small businesses; case prediction could support prioritisation and earlier settlement. Explainable, audited systems could clarify legal reasoning, while translation tools could improve communication with clients whose first language is not English. Multidisciplinary working could develop solicitors’ skills and career satisfaction. Chatbots could extend service hours, and internally developed tools could become services offered to others under firm oversight. The SRA also predicts increasing consumer expectations of technology-enabled services and suggests that failure to adopt AI could become a competitive risk. Its risk claims include biased or discriminatory decisions, fabricated legal authorities and other inaccurate outputs, harm amplified by output scale, confidentiality and privilege breaches, harder-to-detect phishing, and possible false evidence. Firms remain accountable for AI-assisted work, including advice delivered by third-party chatbots. The report advocates augmentation of human judgment rather than its replacement; it does not forecast a quantified reduction in legal employment.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The SRA draws on reported adoption statistics, provider claims, illustrative deployments, external research, regulatory guidance and reported incidents; many prospective benefits are conditional arguments rather than measured legal-market outcomes.
pts.d: The report says that, at the end of the previous year, three quarters of the largest solicitors’ firms used AI, nearly twice the number three years earlier; over 60% of large firms and a third of small firms were at least exploring generative systems. It explicitly describes evidence of growth in small and medium firms as anecdotal. Operational examples include a provider’s claimed 90% case-outcome prediction accuracy; an insurance-claim decision system reportedly taking a third less time than a human and reducing processing costs by 77%; and a contract-management product whose designers claim savings of at least three hours per signing or renewal. These are attributed examples, not SRA-run benchmarks. A banking example describes moving from a 120-person team sampling at most 15% of transactions to AI-supported real-time review of all files. The SRA cites external material for discovery speed and accuracy, worker experience, multidisciplinary teams and business-process savings. Evidence for risks includes the reported submission of nonexistent legal cases, research on trust in computers, privacy incidents and government risk reports. A US mortgage-algorithm example reports a 40% greater likelihood of denying minority ethnic applicants and attributes this to historically biased training decisions; it is a cross-domain illustration, not a measurement of legal AI bias. The referenced dispute over whether evidence could be a deepfake illustrates evidentiary doubt, not proof that the evidence was fabricated. The report also repeats a Goldman Sachs prediction of a 7% global GDP increase over ten years; this is a macroeconomic forecast, not a legal-services productivity estimate. It does not supply quantified evidence of realised access-to-justice improvements or sector-wide employment effects.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The report distinguishes existing uses and reported adoption from open-ended predictions, and makes benefits dependent on appropriate selection, effective use, verification and continuing governance.
pts.d: Published on 20 November 2023, the report presents adoption figures under the framing 'At the end of last year' and describes current deployments alongside products then being introduced. Most legal-market predictions have no fixed date: continued adoption, normalisation of routine automation, stronger consumer expectations and improved commercial availability are anticipated as systems develop. The ten-year GDP forecast is separate from those legal-market predictions. Efficiency and service improvements are qualified by effective use and suitability to individual firms’ needs. Transparency benefits depend on explainable and well-audited systems; improved case planning is particularly associated with prediction systems capable of showing their reasoning. Barriers include procurement and maintenance costs, skills, uncertainty about regulation and client acceptance, limited digitised legal data, and emerging insurance coverage. Commercial products and collaboration may lower barriers but do not remove firms’ obligation to understand data use, supervise systems and check outputs. The SRA says only the largest firms possess enough data to train their own systems. Verification remains necessary even where data access is controlled. Governance must keep pace with output speed and evolving bias. International regulatory differences are described as of the report’s publication, when the EU AI Act and UK approach were still prospective. The SRA also states a plan for a technology-testing sandbox in its 2023–2024 business plan.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted effects extend across firm sizes, solicitors and multidisciplinary staff, commercial and individual clients, courts and the wider public, with benefits and burdens differing by group.
pts.d: Large firms are depicted as early adopters with greater resources and proprietary training data. Smaller firms gain access through commercial and generic tools but face proportionately important cost and skills barriers; senior practitioners without administrative teams may particularly benefit from routine-task automation. Solicitors may redirect time toward complex work and gain skills through collaboration with IT specialists, while retaining verification and accountability responsibilities. Firms may gain productivity, expanded service hours and new revenue opportunities, but also face supervision, insurance, confidentiality and regulatory-management burdens. Commercial clients may manage contracts more efficiently, while lower-income individuals and small businesses could gain access to affordable legal assistance. Clients who do not speak English as a first language may benefit from translation, and consumers more generally may gain faster responses and clearer communication. Conversely, clients may pay for inaccurate products, courts may be misled, and high-volume errors may harm many people at once. Bias could affect criminal defendants, recruitment candidates and people subjected to automated risk classification. International firms and their clients must navigate differing regulatory regimes. The wider justice system could benefit from earlier settlements and improved access, but the report frames these as possibilities rather than demonstrated population-level outcomes.
